items.stem: Suppose raising the federal minimum wage to $15 would raise pay for millions of workers but cost some low-wage jobs. Which comes closest to your view?
items.scope: Assume both effects are real. The question is which tradeoff you'd accept.
options: Raise it to $15 quickly; higher pay for many is worth some lost jobs
Raise it to $15 slowly, over several years, to limit job losses
Raise it only part of the way, or only in areas with high living costs
Don't raise it; lost jobs hurt the least experienced workers most

items.stem: Should workers covered by a union contract be required to pay fees to the union that negotiated it?
items.scope: This is about private-sector jobs. Nobody can be required to join a union.
items.context: 26 states have right-to-work laws, which ban contracts that require these fees.
options: Allow contracts that require fees in every state, overriding state right-to-work laws
Let each state decide, as today
Ban contracts that require fees in every state (a national right-to-work law)

facts.claim: 26 states have right-to-work laws (Michigan repealed its law effective Feb 2024)
facts.source: National Conference of State Legislatures; Michigan Public Act 8 of 2023

definitions.text: A state law that bars union contracts from requiring workers to pay any fees to the union that represents them.

items.stem: How easy should it be for workers to form a union at their workplace?
items.scope: Private-sector workplaces.
options: Much easier: the union is recognized once most workers sign cards, with large fines for employers who interfere
Somewhat easier: faster votes and larger fines for illegal interference
Keep today's rules
Harder: hold new votes every few years for workers to keep the union

items.stem: Should government employees, such as teachers and state office workers, be able to bargain as a group through unions?
items.scope: Police and firefighters aside; think of most government workers.
options: Yes, including the right to strike
Yes, but not to strike
Only over wages, not benefits or work rules
No collective bargaining for government workers

items.stem: Which comes closest to what federal law should do about paid leave for a new child or a serious illness?
items.scope: This is about leave of several weeks, not ordinary sick days.
items.context: Federal law gives many workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave. It does not require paid leave.
options: Guarantee 12 weeks or more of paid leave, funded by a payroll tax
Guarantee a shorter paid leave, such as 4 to 6 weeks
No requirement, but give tax credits to employers who offer paid leave
No federal role; leave it to employers and states

facts.claim: Family and Medical Leave Act (1993) provides up to 12 weeks unpaid job-protected leave to eligible employees; no federal paid-leave mandate

items.stem: Should employers be required to give workers paid sick days?
items.scope: Short-term illness, like the flu.
options: Yes, at least 7 days a year, for all employers
Yes, but only employers with more than 50 workers
No requirement; leave it to states and employers

items.stem: How should the law treat app-based drivers and delivery workers?
items.scope: Think of people who mainly earn a living this way, not people doing it on the side.
options: As employees, with minimum wage, overtime and benefits
A new middle category: pay floors and some benefits, with flexible hours like contractors
As independent contractors, as most are today

items.stem: Which comes closer to your view of rules on business?
items.scope: Think about business regulation in general.

sides.label: Stronger protections
sides.text: Stronger rules to protect workers, consumers and the environment, even if prices rise and fewer businesses start.

sides.label: Fewer rules
sides.text: Fewer rules so businesses grow and prices stay low, even if more workers and consumers are harmed by unsafe practices.

options: Clearly A
Lean A
Lean B
Clearly B

items.stem: When a new kind of product comes along, which approach is closer to your view?
items.scope: Think of new products in general, such as new chemicals, foods or devices.

sides.label: Prove it safe first
sides.text: Companies should show it is safe before selling it, even if that delays useful products for years.

sides.label: Allow first, fix problems
sides.text: Allow it to be sold and deal with problems as they appear, even if some people are harmed first.

options: Clearly A
Lean A
Lean B
Clearly B

items.stem: What should the government do about companies that control most of their market?
items.scope: Think of companies with most of the business in their field, such as online search or meatpacking.
options: Break them up, even if their prices are low
Break them up only if they are proven to hurt consumers, workers or competitors
Leave existing companies alone, but block them from buying rivals
Leave them alone; large size usually reflects success, and new competitors will emerge

items.stem: When two large companies want to merge, how strict should the government be?
items.scope: Think of mergers between companies that sell similar things.
options: Block most large mergers unless the companies prove they will help customers and workers
Review each case and block those likely to raise prices or cut wages
Approve most mergers unless they would clearly raise prices
Rarely interfere; let companies merge as they choose

items.stem: How strict should the rules on large banks be?
items.scope: Banks with more than $100 billion in assets.
options: Much stricter: break up the largest banks
Stricter: make banks hold more of their own money as a cushion against losses
About as strict as today
Looser than today, so banks can lend more

items.stem: If a large bank or company is about to fail and its collapse could hurt the whole economy, what should government do?
items.scope: Think of a failure big enough to cause a recession.
options: Take it over and run it until it can be sold or wound down
Lend it money to survive, with strict conditions, as in 2008
Protect customers' insured deposits only and let the company fail
Let it fail with no government help

items.stem: Which comes closest to your view of requiring a government license to work in jobs like barber, electrician or interior designer?
items.scope: Think about licensing in general, not one job.
items.context: About 1 in 5 US workers holds a government license needed for their job.
options: Require licenses for more jobs, to protect customers
Keep about today's requirements
Require licenses only where health or safety is clearly at risk
Remove most license requirements; customers can rely on reviews and private certifications

facts.claim: About 20-22% of employed people held an active professional certification or license, mostly government-required licenses
facts.source: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Population Survey (certification and licensing)

items.stem: Should government limit how much businesses can charge for essentials like food, water and gas?
items.scope: Think of essentials, not luxuries. Rent is asked about separately.
options: Yes, including caps on prices for essentials when inflation is high
Only after disasters: ban sharp price hikes during declared emergencies
No; high prices draw in more supply and should be allowed, even after disasters

items.stem: Which kind of economy do you think works best?
items.scope: Think about how the economy is organized overall.
options: Most major industries owned by the public or by their workers
Private businesses, but with government running key industries like energy and health care
Private businesses and markets, with strong government rules and a large safety net
Private businesses and markets, with modest rules and a basic safety net
Private businesses and free markets, with as little government as possible

items.stem: Should the government own and run industries like electricity, railroads and internet service?
items.scope: Owned by federal, state or local government, as some cities do with electricity today.
options: Yes, most of them
Some of them, where private companies haven't provided good, affordable service
Only in places with no private provider
No; private companies should run them

items.stem: Should workers at large companies elect some members of the company's board of directors?
items.scope: Companies with more than 1,000 employees. Germany requires this.
options: Yes, about half the board
Yes, about a third of the board
Allow it if companies choose, but don't require it
No

items.subtopic: Noncompete agreements and right to repair
items.stem: Should employers be allowed to make workers agree not to work for a competitor after they leave?
items.scope: Agreements that block a worker from a similar job for a period after leaving.
options: No, ban them for all workers
Only for top executives
Allow them, but limit them to a year or less
Allow them; it's a contract both sides agreed to

items.subtopic: Noncompete agreements and right to repair
items.stem: Should companies be required to make parts, tools and manuals available so owners and independent shops can repair products?
items.scope: Products like phones, cars and farm equipment.
options: Yes, for most products
Only for products where repair matters most, like cars and farm equipment
No; companies should decide

items.stem: What should happen to federal payments and subsidized insurance for farmers?
items.scope: Programs that pay farmers when prices or harvests fall.
options: Expand them
Keep them about as they are
Limit them to small and mid-size farms
Phase them out
items.notes: Expected to cross-cut: opposed by free-market and some left voters, supported in farm regions of both parties.

items.stem: Should states and cities offer tax breaks to persuade companies to build factories or offices there?
items.scope: Deals like tax breaks for a company that brings jobs to an area.
options: Yes, they bring jobs
Only with strict job guarantees and repayment if the company leaves
No; ban these deals

items.stem: Who should decide the interest rates set by the Federal Reserve?
items.scope: Answer for any president of either party.
options: The Federal Reserve alone, with no pressure from elected officials
The Federal Reserve, but Congress should review its decisions more closely
The president should be able to direct the Federal Reserve

items.stem: How much should the federal government spend on roads, bridges, water systems and the power grid?
items.scope: Compared with today. Assume the money is borrowed or comes from taxes.
options: Much more
Somewhat more
About the same
Less; leave more to states and private companies
